content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through designing plugin apis with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns clear method names into a repeatable implementation choice. A jQuery plugin usually extends $.fn, acts on every element in the collection, and returns the collection for chainability. Stateful plugins need deliberate defaults, instance storage, and teardown.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates designing plugin apis using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in designing plugin apis.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: The plugin updates every selected status element and remains chainable.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
summary: Designing Plugin APIs is one part of the building jquery plugins workflow.
